entries.title: Subject pronouns
entries.summary: Who is doing the action. French has two words for 'you' and the choice is social, not grammatical.

rows: 'on' is how people actually say 'we' in speech
clients, strangers, anyone senior to you

entries.pitfall: Using 'tu' with a client reads as rude. At work, default to 'vous' until the other person switches first.

entries.title: être — to be
entries.summary: The most irregular and most used verb in French. Memorise it whole; there is no pattern to derive.
entries.pitfall: 'Je suis' never means 'I am going to' — that is 'je vais'. And 'je suis' is also the 'I follow' form of suivre; context decides.

entries.title: avoir — to have
entries.summary: Second pillar verb. Also the auxiliary for most past tenses, so this table pays for itself in week 6.

rows: Vous avez le mot de passe ?

entries.pitfall: French uses avoir where English uses 'to be' for age, hunger and being right: j'ai 30 ans, j'ai faim, j'ai raison.

entries.title: Articles & noun gender
entries.summary: Every French noun carries a gender. Learn each noun together with its article — 'le bureau', never bare 'bureau'.
entries.pitfall: Gender is not guessable from meaning. 'Un ordinateur' is masculine, 'une souris' feminine — same desk, different genders.

entries.title: Negation — ne … pas
entries.summary: Negation is a sandwich: ne goes before the conjugated verb, pas after it.
entries.pitfall: After a negative, un/une/du/des all collapse to 'de': j'ai un ticket → je n'ai pas **de** ticket. In speech French people drop the 'ne' entirely — 'je comprends pas' — but write it.

entries.title: Regular -ER verbs
entries.summary: About 90% of French verbs. Drop -er, add the ending. Learn this once and you unlock thousands of verbs.
entries.pitfall: -e, -es and -ent are all silent. 'je parle', 'tu parles' and 'ils parlent' sound identical — spelling differs, sound does not.

entries.title: Numbers — the awkward range
entries.summary: French counts normally to 69, then does arithmetic.
entries.pitfall: Belgium and Switzerland use the sane forms septante (70) and nonante (90). France does not — and Odoo's head office being Belgian will not help you here.

entries.title: Regular -IR and -RE verbs
entries.summary: The two smaller regular families. -IR verbs insert -iss- in the plural; -RE verbs mostly just drop the ending.
entries.pitfall: Third-person -RE verbs take no ending at all: 'il attend', not 'il attendt'.

entries.title: Reflexive verbs
entries.summary: Actions you do to yourself. The pronoun changes with the subject and sits before the verb.
entries.pitfall: In the past these take être, not avoir: je **me suis** levé — never 'je m'ai levé'.

entries.title: Possessive adjectives
entries.summary: These agree with the thing owned, not the owner — the opposite of English.
entries.pitfall: 'son' / 'sa' do not tell you the owner's gender. 'Sa solution' is 'his solution' or 'her solution' — only context says which.

entries.title: Partitive articles — some
entries.summary: For unspecified quantities. English usually drops 'some'; French never does.
entries.pitfall: Quantity words take plain 'de': beaucoup **de** clients, assez **d'**argent — never 'beaucoup des clients'.

entries.title: Demonstratives — this / that
entries.summary: French makes no built-in this/that distinction; add -ci or -là only when you must contrast.
entries.pitfall: 'cet' exists purely so you never say 'ce ordinateur' — it is a pronunciation fix, not a new meaning.

entries.title: Passé composé with avoir
entries.summary: The everyday past tense: avoir in the present + a past participle. Used for completed, specific actions.
entries.pitfall: Negation wraps the auxiliary, not the participle: je **n'ai pas** mangé — never 'je n'ai mangé pas'.

entries.title: Irregular past participles
entries.summary: The frequent verbs are the irregular ones. These twelve cover most of what you will write.
entries.pitfall: comprendre and apprendre follow prendre: compris, appris.

entries.title: Passé composé with être
entries.summary: A closed set of movement and state-change verbs takes être instead of avoir — and their participle agrees with the subject.
entries.pitfall: All reflexives take être too: je me suis douché. The memory hook for the set is DR MRS VANDERTRAMP.

entries.title: Three ways to ask a question
entries.summary: Same meaning, three registers. Pick by how formal the situation is.
entries.pitfall: Question words go first in all three: Pourquoi est-ce que…? / Pourquoi avez-vous…? Use inversion in support emails — it reads as professional.

entries.title: Futur proche — the near future
entries.summary: aller in the present + an unchanged infinitive. Covers almost everything English says with 'going to' or 'will'.
entries.pitfall: The second verb never conjugates: 'je vais envoyer', never 'je vais envoie'.

entries.title: Direct object pronouns
entries.summary: Replace a noun already known from context. They sit before the verb, which feels backwards in English.
entries.pitfall: In the near future the pronoun goes before the infinitive: je vais **le** résoudre.

entries.title: Imparfait — the background past
entries.summary: One stem rule, no exceptions except être: take the nous form of the present, drop -ons, add the endings.
entries.pitfall: être is the single irregular stem: ét- → j'étais, tu étais, il était. Everything else derives from the nous form.

entries.title: Imparfait vs passé composé
entries.summary: The hardest distinction at A2. Imparfait is the scenery; passé composé is what happened.

rows: single events — j'ai résolu le ticket
something that interrupts — le serveur est tombé

entries.pitfall: They combine constantly: 'Je **travaillais** quand le serveur **est tombé**' — background in imparfait, interruption in passé composé.

entries.title: Comparatives & superlatives
entries.summary: plus / moins / aussi … que. Two irregular forms spoil an otherwise clean system.
entries.pitfall: 'plus bon' does not exist — it is 'meilleur'. Adjective describes a noun (meilleur), adverb describes a verb (mieux).

entries.title: Indirect object pronouns
entries.summary: For people you do something *to*: lui and leur. The giveaway is a verb built with 'à'.

rows: Je téléphone au client → Je **lui** téléphone.
Je réponds aux clients → Je **leur** réponds.

entries.pitfall: 'lui' covers both him and her. Verbs needing it: téléphoner à, répondre à, parler à, demander à, envoyer à.

entries.title: Conditional politeness
entries.summary: Two conditional forms turn a demand into a request. In support work these are not optional.
entries.pitfall: 'Je veux' lands as entitled to French ears. Default to 'je voudrais' with anyone you do not know well.

entries.title: Relative pronouns — qui / que
entries.summary: Both become 'who', 'which' or 'that' in English. The test is what comes next in French.
entries.pitfall: 'que' elides to 'qu'' before a vowel: le problème **qu'**il a signalé. 'qui' never elides.
